title: Hosea 7:8–16
context: The LORD turns from court intrigue to Ephraim’s foreign entanglements. Ephraim “mixes himself among the nations” and is “a pancake not turned over,” half-done through compromise (7:8). Foreigners drain his strength, and gray hairs appear, yet “he doesn’t realize it” (7:9). Pride testifies against Israel, as in 5:5, and still they do not return (7:10). Ephraim is like “an easily deceived dove,” calling to Egypt and going to Assyria (7:11); many readers connect this with the shifting policy of the northern kingdom’s last kings (compare 2 Kings 17:4), a background held with caution. The LORD will spread his net over them (7:12). He laments, “Though I would redeem them, yet they have spoken lies against me” (7:13); the site’s existing discussion at Matthew 23:37 treats the question this line raises about God’s desire and human refusal, and these notes point there rather than restating it. The people howl on their beds rather than crying to the LORD with their hearts, and they return, “but not to the Most High” (7:14–16). The final line turns Egypt, the place they sought for help, into the place of their derision. Shared ground: both traditions read the passage as a warning against misplaced trust and repentance that never reaches the LORD.

verses.text: Ephraim mixes himself among the nations. Ephraim is a pancake not turned over.
verses.arminianNotes: “Ephraim mixes himself among the nations. Ephraim is a pancake not turned over.” Arminian readers see the cost of compromise: by mixing with the nations Ephraim has become half-done, burned on one side and raw on the other, through choices that divided his loyalty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image as spiritual incompleteness, a people outwardly religious yet inwardly unformed by the LORD. Shared ground: both traditions read “mixes himself” as political alliance and religious assimilation together, and both see the unturned cake as a picture of a life left half-finished through neglect of God.

verses.text: Strangers have devoured his strength, and he doesn’t realize it. Indeed, gray hairs are here and there on him, and he doesn’t realize it.
verses.arminianNotes: “Strangers have devoured his strength, and he doesn’t realize it.” Arminian readers see the tragedy of decline that goes unnoticed, itself a fruit of neglecting God; awareness is the first step toward repentance, and Ephraim lacks it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see spiritual blindness as part of the judgment: the gray hairs of decay appear “here and there on him,” yet Ephraim cannot perceive them. Shared ground: both traditions read the repeated “he doesn’t realize it” as a warning about the deceitfulness of gradual decline, and both see foreign powers draining the strength Israel sought from them.

verses.text: The pride of Israel testifies to his face; yet they haven’t returned to the LORD their God, nor sought him, for all this.
verses.arminianNotes: “The pride of Israel testifies to his face” repeats the opening of 5:5. Arminian readers stress the words “for all this”: despite discipline, the people have not returned to the LORD or sought him, which shows that affliction alone does not compel repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see pride as the persistent root that discipline exposes but does not by itself remove, and they read the refusal to return as confirming the bondage described in 5:4. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as evidence that judgment without a changed heart does not produce return, and both hold that the fault lies with Israel’s pride.

verses.text: “Ephraim is like an easily deceived dove, without understanding. They call to Egypt. They go to Assyria.
verses.arminianNotes: “Ephraim is like an easily deceived dove, without understanding. They call to Egypt. They go to Assyria.” Arminian readers see a nation that has abandoned discernment, flitting between powers in its own strength and responsible for choices that bring ruin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the dove’s senselessness as the fruit of having forsaken the knowledge of God, so that political cleverness becomes folly. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an indictment of trusting foreign alliances instead of the LORD, and many readers connect it with the northern kingdom’s shifting policy toward Egypt and Assyria (compare 2 Kings 17:4), a link held with caution.

verses.text: When they go, I will spread my net on them. I will bring them down like the birds of the sky. I will chastise them, as their congregation has heard.
verses.arminianNotes: “When they go, I will spread my net on them.” The LORD turns the bird image into judgment. Arminian readers see the LORD responding to the people’s going, so that the net falls on the path they chose, and they note that the chastisement matches what “their congregation has heard” in earlier warnings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the LORD is the hunter: whatever the nations do, the net is his, and “I will chastise them” expresses his sovereign discipline. Shared ground: both traditions read the net as covenant judgment announced in advance and carried out by the LORD, and both acknowledge that the exact sense of the last line is uncertain.

verses.text: Woe to them! For they have wandered from me. Destruction to them! For they have trespassed against me. Though I would redeem them, yet they have spoken lies against me.
verses.arminianNotes: “Though I would redeem them, yet they have spoken lies against me.” Arminian readers see here a sincere desire to redeem that the people resisted, and they compare Jesus’ lament over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37) as another picture of grace offered and refused.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm the sincerity of the LORD’s desire and the people’s full guilt, and they read the verse within God’s larger purpose in judgment and salvation. Shared ground: both traditions take the lament with full weight and see the woe as just; whether such grace can be finally resisted is treated in the existing discussion at Matthew 23:37, which this verse closely resembles.

verses.text: They haven’t cried to me with their heart, but they howl on their beds. They assemble themselves for grain and new wine. They turn away from me.
verses.arminianNotes: “They haven’t cried to me with their heart, but they howl on their beds.” Arminian readers see the difference between distress and repentance: the people wail over their losses and gather for grain and wine, but their hearts do not turn to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see crying out without the heart as the mark of religion concerned with provisions rather than with God himself. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as distinguishing heartfelt prayer from complaint, and both note that assembling “for grain and new wine” may reflect rites aimed at the harvest, though the precise practice is uncertain.

verses.text: Though I have taught and strengthened their arms, yet they plot evil against me.
verses.arminianNotes: “Though I have taught and strengthened their arms, yet they plot evil against me.” Arminian readers see grace given and repaid with rebellion: the LORD trained and empowered his people, and they turned his gifts against him by their own choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the ingratitude of a people whose strength came wholly from God, and they see the plotting as the depth of sin. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a portrait of divine kindness met with treachery, and both see the people’s evil as their own, set against the steady goodness of the LORD toward them.

verses.text: They return, but not to the Most High. They are like a faulty bow. Their princes will fall by the sword for the rage of their tongue. This will be their derision in the land of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: “They return, but not to the Most High. They are like a faulty bow.” Arminian readers see turning that is real movement but in the wrong direction, like a bow that fails at the moment of shooting and proves unreliable when it matters most.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see false repentance that changes direction without coming to God, and they read the princes’ fall as judgment on “the rage of their tongue.” Shared ground: both traditions read “This will be their derision in the land of Egypt” as ironic, since the Egypt they sought for help becomes the place of their shame.
